The Liberal Order in Retreat: An Israeli Radio Conversation on the New World Disorder

A measured discussion between Dr. Oren Nahari and Professor Benjamin Miller offers a lucid account of the weakening post-1945 order and the harsher logic emerging in its place.
By Amnon Sussman
13-04-2026

This article is based on an interview conducted in Hebrew on the Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, as part of the program “Shabbat with Oren Nahari”, and directed primarily at an Israeli audience. In that sense, the conversation was not merely an abstract discussion of international relations. It was also an effort to interpret a rapidly changing global order for listeners in Israel, a country whose strategic position makes such changes unusually immediate and consequential.

In an era dominated by noise, fragmentation, and rhetorical excess, the conversation between Dr. Oren Nahari and Professor Benjamin Miller stood out for its sobriety. It was a measured exchange, intellectually disciplined and historically grounded, yet its conclusions were anything but reassuring. What emerged from the discussion was a clear and disturbing proposition: the liberal international order that shaped much of the post-1945 world is weakening profoundly, and no stable moral or institutional replacement has yet taken its place.

Nahari, one of Israel’s most experienced journalists and public intellectual broadcasters, framed the discussion with a long historical arc. He began where any serious inquiry into world order must begin: with the settlement of 1945, the bipolarity of the Cold War, and the brief unipolar moment of American predominance after the fall of the Soviet Union. His central question was simple: what kind of world are we living in now? Professor Miller’s answer was equally direct. The dominant logic of the present era, he argued, is no longer liberalism but nationalism—often revisionist nationalism, willing to challenge borders and justify expansion in the language of historical entitlement, cultural unity, or civilizational destiny.

That diagnosis immediately placed Russia’s war against Ukraine at the center of the conversation. Miller pointed to the ideological structure of Vladimir Putin’s argument: the claim that Ukrainians are essentially Russians, that Ukraine belongs within a historical Russian sphere, and that territorial aggression can therefore be reframed as rectification rather than conquest. The same logic, he suggested, hovers over the question of Taiwan, where Beijing invokes history and identity in order to delegitimize the island’s separate political existence. What matters here is not merely military ambition, but the return of a political vocabulary that had supposedly been discredited: history over law, ethnicity over sovereignty, power over norm.

One of the most important concepts in the interview was that of spheres of influence. Miller treated this not as a relic of nineteenth-century diplomacy, but as a principle that may once again be structuring the international system. During the Cold War, he noted, a de facto division of Europe into American and Soviet zones helped prevent direct great-power war, even as it denied smaller nations meaningful autonomy. Nahari sharpened this point by invoking the Cuban missile crisis, when the United States effectively asserted that proximity and strategic geography still mattered decisively even in the nuclear age. The implication was unmistakable: the emerging order may not be chaotic. It may be highly structured—but according to a harsher grammar, in which major powers define what smaller states must endure.

The discussion then moved inward, toward the West itself. Here Miller made one of his most compelling arguments: the liberal order is being challenged not only by external authoritarian powers such as Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea, but also by internal populist-nationalist currents within Western societies. In the American case, he traced the rise of Trumpism to structural grievances produced by globalization, deindustrialization, migration, and the human costs of foreign military interventions. Large segments of American society, especially outside the coastal metropolitan centers, no longer experience the liberal order as a source of prosperity, dignity, or protection. Trump did not create this resentment, but he recognized and mobilized it with extraordinary effectiveness.

Nahari then posed a question that cut to the philosophical core of the matter: does Donald Trump still see himself as part of “the West” in its traditional sense? The question is crucial because it suggests that the crisis may not simply be one of declining Western power, but of changing Western self-definition. In the older conception, the West was a political and normative community: liberal, democratic, institutionally minded, and at least rhetorically committed to universal principles. In the newer nationalist imagination described in the interview, “the West” becomes something narrower and more tribal: white, Christian, culturally defensive, suspicious of immigration and pluralism, and less interested in alliance systems built around shared rules.

At this point, the interview approached Samuel Huntington’s “clash of civilizations,” but in a transformed version. Miller suggested that parts of the Trumpist world no longer view liberal Europe as a natural civilizational ally. Instead, they may feel a degree of cultural affinity with Putin’s Russia—not because Russia is liberal, but precisely because it is perceived as traditionalist, Christian, nationalist, and resistant to progressive cultural change. This inversion is one of the most striking features of the present moment. It helps explain how sympathy for Russia, hostility toward liberal Europe, and ambivalence about long-standing Western alliances can coexist within the same political current.

Israel entered the discussion not as a peripheral case but as a revealing test of these new alignments. On one side, Israel can be seen by the civilizational right in the United States as a frontline state in a broader struggle against radical Islam, and therefore as a natural ally deserving strong support. On the other side, the “America First” tendency within that same political universe asks why the United States should bear strategic or military costs for conflicts outside its immediate national sphere. This tension is of direct relevance to Israeli listeners, because it suggests that support for Israel within the American right is neither conceptually uniform nor strategically guaranteed. It may depend on which version of nationalism prevails: civilizational solidarity or hard-edged noninterventionism.

The sharpest moment in the conversation came toward its conclusion, when Nahari asked what concrete sign would indicate that the old liberal order had effectively come to an end. Miller’s answer was notable for its precision. Such a sign, he implied, would not be rhetorical but practical: an American-Russian arrangement over Ukraine’s head; pressure on Kyiv to accept concessions that would compromise its long-term sovereignty; and above all, a failure by the United States to commit clearly to the defense of Taiwan. Taiwan, in this framework, is more than a geopolitical flashpoint. It is a test case. If Washington proves unwilling to defend a prosperous liberal democracy under pressure from a great authoritarian power, then the claim that the United States still serves as the guardian of the liberal order becomes difficult to sustain.

What made this interview especially valuable was not merely the substance of the claims, but the mode of argument. There was no theatricality, no apocalyptic flourish, and no reduction of international politics to slogans. Instead, the conversation performed a rarer public service: it offered conceptual clarity. It gave listeners a framework for understanding that the present international crisis is not just a sequence of isolated events—Ukraine, Trump, Taiwan, Russia, China—but a deeper transformation in the principles by which the world is being organized.

For an Israeli audience, this matters acutely. Israel is both observer and participant in the transition. Its security has long depended not only on material alliances, but also on the assumptions embedded in a particular international order: American centrality, Western cohesion, and a broad if uneven commitment to the defense of democratic allies. If those assumptions are eroding, then Israelis are not merely watching a distant global drama. They are living inside its consequences.

The conversation between Dr. Oren Nahari and Professor Benjamin Miller therefore deserves attention beyond the immediate news cycle. It illuminated, with unusual composure, a historical threshold. The world built after 1945 is not disappearing overnight, but its normative authority is fading, its institutions are losing coherence, and its leading power is showing signs of strategic and ideological withdrawal. What comes next may well be more openly transactional, more civilizational in tone, more tolerant of coercion, and less constrained by universalist language. That is not yet a settled order. But it is already the atmosphere in which the next order is being formed.
